title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 95–96
description: Reviewed upper-intermediate register choices: formal and neutral alternatives, notices, shortened informal British vocabulary and slang.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Sections, comparative word scales, illustrated notices, informal examples, exercises and corresponding answer-key entries checked for register and vocabulary targets.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA supplied where reasonably reliable; longer or uncertain expressions have blank IPA rather than guesses. Regional or stylistic differences are described in notes.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked the teaching pages, illustrations, exercise pages and answer key; authored original examples; reviewed register labels, idiomatic use, translation, schema, IDs, and static word/sentence audio compatibility.
audit.limitations: No live VocabLab import, browser TTS, speech recognition, word-audio playback or round-trip UI test was performed; audio assets are not bundled.

units.title: Unit 95 — Formal and informal words 1
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 196–197 (PDF pages 197–198).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Understand how register, audience and relationships influence word choice.
Contrast formal, neutral and informal equivalents without assuming they are interchangeable in every context.
Recognise formal academic phrases and official notice vocabulary.
Identify common British informal words and replace them appropriately in formal writing.

sectionsChecked: C: Words of Latin and Greek origin
E: Formality in notices, instructions, etc.

items.example: The formality of your message should suit its audience.
items.note: The level of formality depends on the relationship and the communication situation.

items.example: Formal language is usually appropriate in an official complaint.
items.note: Can signal respect, politeness, distance or academic style.

items.example: Informal language is natural when chatting with close friends.
items.note: Can signal friendliness or closeness; it is not automatically better or more fluent.

items.example: The inheritance was divided equally among her offspring.
items.note: Formal term for a person’s children; the same form can be singular or plural.

items.example: The couple have three children.
items.note: Neutral equivalent of offspring; more appropriate than kids in many formal contexts.

items.example: The kids are playing in the garden.
items.note: Informal alternative to children; fine in everyday conversation.

items.example: The historical register recorded the family’s last abode.
items.note: A rather formal or literary way to refer to someone’s home.

items.example: Applicants must provide their current address of residence.
items.note: Formal word for a place where someone lives.

items.example: We finally arrived home after midnight.
items.note: Ordinary neutral term for the place where you live.

items.example: She rented a small flat close to the station.
items.note: Neutral British English word for an apartment.

items.example: Why don’t you come over to my place for dinner?
items.note: In this informal use, my place means my home.

items.example: At the end of the ceremony, the visitors said goodbye.
items.note: More formal or emphatic than bye.

items.example: Bye, I’ll see you tomorrow morning.
items.note: Common everyday farewell.

items.example: Bye-bye, see you at the weekend!
items.note: Warm, very informal goodbye; can sound childlike in some settings.

items.example: Cheerio, everyone; enjoy the rest of your day!
items.note: Informal British farewell; not used much in many other varieties of English.

items.pt: dar errado; não sair como esperado (formal)
items.example: Something went amiss during the database migration.
items.note: Fairly formal expression meaning go wrong; compare go pear-shaped.

items.example: If anything goes wrong, please call the support team.
items.note: Neutral equivalent of go amiss or go pear-shaped.

items.example: Our weekend plans went pear-shaped when the car broke down.
items.note: Informal British expression meaning develop badly or fail.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The technician responded immediately to the warning.
items.note: More formal than right away; at once is a neutral alternative.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: Please send the revised schedule at once.
items.note: Neutral alternative to immediately in the sense of without delay.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: I’ll call you right away when the package arrives.
items.note: Conversational alternative to immediately.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The researchers utilise advanced imaging techniques.
items.note: Formal alternative to use; British spelling with -ise, US often utilize.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: Software updates are released frequently.
items.note: Slightly more formal than often.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The error may occur when two requests arrive together.
items.note: Formal equivalent of happen; often used in reports and academic texts.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The study established a clear relationship between the variables.
items.note: In research writing, establish can mean demonstrate or prove a link.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The service provides subscribers with a detailed monthly report.
items.note: Pattern: provide somebody with something; give is usually less formal.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The team attempted to recover the missing records.
items.note: Attempt to do something is more formal than try to do something.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: The commission seeks further evidence before reaching a decision.
items.note: Seek something is formal; seek–sought–sought is irregular.

items.section: C · Formal words of Latin or Greek origin
items.example: Understanding safety requirements is fundamental to the design.
items.note: More formal than basic in many academic contexts.

items.pt: em termos de; no que diz respeito a
items.example: The options differ in terms of cost and reliability.
items.note: Formal phrase introducing the aspect being considered.

items.example: First-year students, in particular, need clear instructions.
items.note: Highlights a specific example or group within a broader category.

items.example: The outdoor event was postponed on account of heavy rain.
items.note: Formal alternative to because of.

items.example: The panel selected candidates on the basis of their experience.
items.note: Formal phrase specifying the grounds or criteria for a decision.

items.pt: em relação a; a respeito de
items.example: The manager asked a question in relation to the budget.
items.note: Formal phrase meaning concerning or with reference to.

items.example: The emergency stairway must remain clear.
items.note: More formal than stairs; often found in signs and building notices.

items.example: The side entrance will remain closed until further notice.
items.note: Common official notice: the arrangement continues until a new announcement.

items.example: Passengers must not alight while the vehicle is moving.
items.note: Formal transport word meaning get off; usually found in notices.

items.example: Please remain seated while the train is in motion.
items.note: Formal notice wording for when a vehicle is moving.

items.pt: dirigir a palavra a; falar com alguém (formal)
items.example: Visitors should address any questions to reception.
items.note: In notices, do not address the driver means do not speak to the driver.

items.example: Wait until the bus is stationary before getting off.
items.note: Stationary means not moving; not to be confused with stationery, writing materials.

items.example: The venue has a seating capacity of four hundred.
items.note: On a notice, capacity may state a maximum safe number of people or weight.

items.example: The lift is limited to eight persons.
items.note: Formal plural used in regulations; people is the usual neutral plural.

items.example: Visitors may deposit large bags at the entrance.
items.note: Formal verb meaning leave an item for storage or safekeeping.

items.example: Tickets must be paid for in advance.
items.note: Fixed phrase for doing something before the relevant event.

items.example: We regret that this service is temporarily unavailable.
items.note: Formal way to express apology or bad news in public notices.

items.example: Customers can purchase tickets online.
items.note: More formal than buy, particularly in written notices.

items.example: Passengers may board the train at platform four.
items.note: Opposite of alight in transport announcements.

items.example: We took the lift to the sixth floor.
items.note: The usual British term for an elevator; appears in a capacity notice.

items.example: Any articles left in storage must be collected by Friday.
items.note: In notices, an article can mean an individual object or item, not just a written article.

items.example: The charity no longer accepts payment by cheque.
items.note: British spelling of check in the banking sense; not used for a routine inspection.

items.example: The notice says the maximum load is five hundred kilos.
items.note: Max is an abbreviation of maximum, commonly seen in signs and limits.

items.example: I had a quick kip before my evening shift.
items.note: Informal British noun or verb relating to sleep.

items.example: She went on holiday with an old pal from school.
items.note: Casual alternative to friend.

items.example: A mate from work helped me move house.
items.note: Very common informal word for friend in British English.

items.example: I need to swot for tomorrow’s chemistry exam.
items.note: British informal verb for studying hard; also a noun for a studious person.

items.example: Ta for the lift; I really appreciate it.
items.note: Very informal British expression of thanks; avoid in professional messages.

items.example: My brainy cousin solved the puzzle in minutes.
items.note: Informal equivalent of intelligent or clever.

items.example: That smell from the rubbish bin is gross.
items.note: Informal adjective meaning disgusting or unpleasant in this sense.

items.example: I would not buy equipment from that dodgy website.
items.note: British informal adjective for unreliable, dishonest or doubtful things.

units.title: Unit 96 — Formal and informal words 2
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 198–199 (PDF pages 199–200).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Understand how clipped and monosyllabic English words signal informal register.
Distinguish everyday shortened forms from strongly informal slang.
Interpret British English slang for money, food, people and occupations without using offensive labels carelessly.
Recognise -y and -ie informal shortenings and replace them with neutral alternatives when appropriate.

items.example: The cops arrived shortly after the alarm went off.
items.note: Informal word for police officers; police is more neutral.

items.example: The loos are at the end of the corridor.
items.note: British informal plural of loo; neutral alternative: toilets.

items.example: The concert ticket cost forty quid.
items.note: Informal unit meaning pound sterling; often unchanged after numbers.

items.example: We roasted some spuds with rosemary for lunch.
items.note: Informal term for potatoes; especially British English.

items.example: I cycle to work on my old bike.
items.note: Common everyday shortened word for bicycle; can also mean motorcycle in context.

items.example: We took the tube to the museum.
items.note: In this transport sense, the London Underground; not a general word for all metros.

items.example: The criminal spent several months in the nick.
items.note: British slang for prison; very informal, not suitable in formal reports.

items.example: We booked a cab to the airport.
items.note: Common conversational alternative to taxi.

items.example: Lab is a clipping of laboratory.
items.note: Word-formation term for shortening a longer word.

items.example: The samples are being tested in the lab.
items.note: Shortened form of laboratory, accepted in many contexts.

items.example: She joined a tech company last year.
items.note: Shortened form of technology; very common in business conversation.

items.example: There was an interesting documentary on the telly.
items.note: Very informal British shortened word for television.

items.example: He picked up a cycling mag at the station.
items.note: Informal shortened form of magazine.

items.example: We saw an ad for a new language course.
items.note: Informal shortening of advertisement; common in both UK and US English.

items.example: She replied to a job advert on Monday.
items.note: Shortened form of advertisement, especially British usage.

items.example: I read about the election in the local paper.
items.note: Here paper is short for newspaper; paper has other meanings.

items.example: I left my mobile at home this morning.
items.note: Shortened form of mobile phone; in US English, cell phone is common.

items.example: I’ll phone you when I reach the hotel.
items.note: Shortened form of telephone, commonly used as a noun or verb.

items.example: Please put the yoghurt back in the fridge.
items.note: Common clipping of refrigerator; spelling includes d before ge.

items.example: The vet examined our cat and gave us advice.
items.note: Short for veterinary surgeon; common neutral usage in conversation.

items.example: The small town has become popular with celebs.
items.note: Informal shortening of celebrity.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: Slang can sound out of place in a job interview.
items.note: Very informal vocabulary that varies by group, place and time.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: He spent all his dosh on a new computer.
items.note: British slang for money; recognise it rather than using it in formal contexts.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: She had enough readies to pay for lunch.
items.note: Informal British expression for available cash.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: We need more moolah before we can buy a van.
items.note: Informal slang for money; not appropriate in official writing.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: There was plenty of nosh at the celebration.
items.note: British slang for food; often used casually.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: The café serves decent grub at low prices.
items.note: Informal word for food; not generally a word for a formal menu.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: I grabbed a cheese sarnie between meetings.
items.note: British informal short form of sandwich.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: Would you like a cuppa before we go?
items.note: In British English, typically a cup of tea.

items.pt: nerd; pessoa muito dedicada a temas técnicos
items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: He calls himself a history nerd and reads about it every day.
items.note: Informal term that may be affectionate or derogatory depending on tone.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: She is a photography geek who knows every camera setting.
items.note: Often used positively by enthusiasts, but can also be dismissive.

items.pt: aficionado obsessivo; especialista excessivamente detalhista (gíria britânica)
items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: He is a railway anorak who memorises old timetables.
items.note: British slang for someone with an unusually detailed niche enthusiasm; can sound unkind.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: I would not trust that quack with my health.
items.note: Derogatory word for an incompetent or dishonest doctor; not a respectful neutral synonym.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: The character talks to his shrink once a week.
items.note: Informal slang often referring to a psychiatrist or therapist; can be dismissive.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: The old bill arrived before anyone left the scene.
items.note: Informal British slang for the police; may sound dated.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: The documentary interviewed a former squaddie.
items.note: British informal word for a low-ranking soldier.

items.pt: vocabulário passivo; palavras que se reconhecem mas não se usam ativamente
items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: Learners can keep rare slang in their passive vocabulary.
items.note: Words you can recognise or understand without needing to use them yourself.

items.section: C · Slang for money, food and people
items.example: The story received a lot of attention in the tabloid press.
items.note: Popular press sometimes uses slang for vivid or sensational writing.

items.example: They worked every weekend to earn some bread.
items.note: Slang sense meaning money, not the food; appears among possible informal alternatives in the answer key.

items.example: We stopped for brekkie before catching the train.
items.note: Informal form of breakfast.

items.example: We invited the neighbours over for a barbie.
items.note: Informal form of barbecue, especially Australian English.

items.example: Would you like a biccy with your tea?
items.note: British informal shortening of biscuit.

items.example: She came to the event with her hubby.
items.note: Informal affectionate form of husband; not appropriate in formal writing.

items.example: She showed us some piccies from her holiday.
items.note: Informal plural of piccy, from picture.

items.example: There are several veggie dishes on the menu.
items.note: Informal form of vegetarian, often used as an adjective for food.

items.example: The brickie finished the garden wall yesterday.
items.note: British colloquial shortening of bricklayer; caption in exercise 96.4.
